# Encephalitis

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Infectious diseases > Infections of the central nervous system > Encephalitis*

[Original Article Link](/library/rs0fwh)

---

## Summary

Encephalitis is the inflammation of <u>brain</u> <u>parenchyma</u> with neurological dysfunction. <u>Infectious encephalitis</u> is caused by viral (most common), bacterial, parasitic, or fungal pathogens. <u>Autoimmune encephalitis</u> is associated with the production of <u>autoantibodies</u> to neuronal <u>antigens</u> and is often paraneoplastic. <u>Prodromal</u> symptoms include <u>fever</u>, <u>headache</u>, and <u>nausea</u>, with progression to neurological and psychiatric symptoms within hours to weeks, including <u>altered mental status</u>, <u>seizures</u>, <u>focal neurological deficits</u>, <u>hallucinations</u>, and <u>psychosis</u>. Diagnosis is based on <u>laboratory studies</u> (<u>serology</u>, <u>CSF analysis</u>) and <u>brain</u> <u>MRI</u>. Initial testing includes serum and <u>CSF</u> <u>tests for common and treatable causes of encephalitis</u>. Additional testing is guided by clinical features and epidemiological clues (e.g., season, geographic location, travel, and exposure history). Evaluation for <u>malignancy</u> is indicated in all patients with proven or suspected <u>autoimmune encephalitis</u>. <u>Brain biopsy</u> may be considered if the cause of encephalitis remains unknown. <u>Empiric antimicrobial therapy for encephalitis</u> is initiated immediately in all patients and always includes IV <u>acyclovir</u>. <u>Empiric antibiotic therapy for bacterial meningitis</u> and <u>doxycycline</u> to cover for tick-borne infections may be added based on clinical suspicion. <u>Antimicrobial therapy</u> is tailored once an infectious cause has been identified. Immunomodulatory treatment for <u>autoimmune encephalitis</u> may be considered once infectious causes have been excluded.

---

## Definitions

* Encephalitis: inflammation of <u>brain</u> <u>parenchyma</u> with neurological dysfunction

* Cerebellitis: inflammation of the <u>cerebellum</u>

* Brainstem encephalitis: inflammation of the <u>brainstem</u> and adjacent regions

* Meningoencephalitis: concurrent inflammation of <u>meninges</u> (<u>meningitis</u>) and <u>brain</u> <u>parenchyma</u> (encephalitis)

* Encephalomyelitis: concurrent inflammation of the <u>brain</u> (encephalitis) and spinal cord (<u>myelitis</u>)

---

## Overview

There is substantial overlap in the <u>clinical features of encephalitis</u> from different causes. See “<u>Diagnosis of encephalitis</u>” and “<u>Management of encephalitis</u>” for the initial approach to all patients.




> [!WARNING]
> Consult infectious diseases and begin <u>empiric antimicrobial therapy for encephalitis</u> without delay until a treatable infectious cause of encephalitis is ruled out.




> [!WARNING]
> <u>Treat acute seizures</u> and begin <u>management of elevated intracranial pressure</u> during the <u>primary survey</u>.

---

## Clinical features

* Progression: acute (hours to days) or subacute (days to weeks)

* Nonspecific <u>prodromal</u> symptoms (hours to weeks prior)

* <u>Fever</u>

* <u>Headache</u>

* <u>Nausea</u>

* Neurological

* <u>Altered mental status</u>

* <u>Memory</u> loss

* <u>Seizures</u> (focal or generalized)

* <u>Focal neurological deficits</u> 

* <u>Hemiparesis</u>

* <u>Hyperreflexia</u>

* <u>Cranial nerve palsies</u>

* Language dysfunction (e.g., <u>aphasia</u>, <u>dysarthria</u>)

* <u>Extrapyramidal symptoms</u>

* <u>Dysautonomia</u>

* Psychiatric

* Behavioral changes (e.g., hypersexuality, <u>hypomania</u>, <u>agitation</u>)

* <u>Hallucinations</u>

* <u>Anxiety</u>

* <u>Psychosis</u>





> [!TIP]
> Subacute onset of psychiatric symptoms in combination with <u>seizures</u> and/or <u>focal neurological deficits</u> should raise clinical suspicion for encephalitis.

---

## Diagnosis

Suspect encephalitis in any patient with <u>altered mental status</u> of unknown cause.




### Approach [[2]](/library/R9YlMr)[[3]](/library/vfdAL60)[[5]](/library/Ph1WVg0)




* Clinical evaluation

* Evaluate for <u>clinical features of encephalitis</u> and perform a thorough <u>neurological examination</u>.

* Identify <u>risk factors for infectious encephalitis</u>.

* Identify causes of <u>autoimmune encephalitis</u>, e.g., underlying <u>malignancy</u>.

* Identify clinical features of underlying conditions (see “<u>Overview of encephalitis</u>”).

* Exclude <u>differential diagnoses of encephalitis</u>.

* Initial investigations (all patients)

* Routine <u>laboratory studies</u> (<u>CBC</u>, <u>CMP</u>, <u>blood cultures</u>) and <u>HIV testing</u>

* <u>Lumbar puncture</u> (<u>LP</u>) if no <u>contraindications to LP</u>  [[5]](/library/Ph1WVg0)

* <u>Brain</u> imaging (ideally <u>MRI</u> with IV contrast)

* <u>EEG</u>

* Serum and <u>CSF</u> <u>tests for common and treatable causes of encephalitis</u>

* Additional investigations

* Freeze <u>CSF</u> samples for further testing.

* Consult infectious diseases and <u>neurology</u> for guidance on <u>additional investigations for encephalitis</u>.





> [!WARNING]
> Do not delay empiric treatment; initiate diagnostic and treatment steps in parallel.




### Initial <u>laboratory studies</u> [[2]](/library/R9YlMr)[[3]](/library/vfdAL60)[[4]](/library/JSds0p0)




#### Routine tests




* Basic blood tests: <u>CBC</u>, <u>coagulation panel</u>, <u>CMP</u>

* <u>HIV testing</u> (e.g., <u>fourth-generation HIV test</u>): Obtain in all patients.  [[5]](/library/Ph1WVg0)

* <u>CSF analysis</u>

* Typical findings in viral and <u>autoimmune encephalitis</u>

* <u>Opening pressure</u>: may be normal or elevated [[7]](/library/xgdEx60)

* Cell count: <u>WBC</u> > 5/mmÂ³; typically <u>increased lymphocytes</u> (<u>lymphocytic</u> <u>pleocytosis</u>)

* Protein: normal to moderately increased

* <u>Glucose</u>: normal (approx. two-thirds of blood <u>glucose</u> level)

* See also “<u>CSF analysis in meningitis</u>” and “<u>CSF analysis in HSV encephalitis</u>.”





> [!WARNING]
> A normal <u>CSF analysis</u> does not exclude encephalitis. [[2]](/library/R9YlMr)




#### Infectious and immune studies [[3]](/library/vfdAL60)




Studies include initial universal testing for common and treatable causes of encephalitis.  [[3]](/library/vfdAL60)[[4]](/library/JSds0p0)




* Studies in blood and serum

* <u>Blood cultures</u> (two sets): Obtain before starting <u>antibiotic therapy</u>.

* <u>Serological studies for syphilis</u>: e.g., <u>RPR</u> or <u>treponemal testing</u>

* <u>West Nile virus</u> <u>IgM antibody</u> (seasonal)

* <u>Anti-NMDAR antibodies</u>

* Serum <u>IgG</u>

* Residence in or travel to <u>endemic</u> areas: <u>serological testing</u> for <u>Borrelia</u>, <u>Rickettsia</u>, <u>Ehrlichia</u>, and <u>Anaplasma</u> species

* Studies in <u>CSF</u>

* <u>CSF</u> cultures and <u>Gram stain</u>

* <u>PCR</u>

* Single viral <u>PCR</u> tests for <u>HSV-1</u>, <u>HSV-2</u>, <u>VZV</u>, and <u>enteroviruses</u>  [[3]](/library/vfdAL60)

* Or, if available, <u>multiplex PCR</u> <u>meningitis</u>/encephalitis panel

* Tests for other infections: <u>VDRL</u>, <u>cryptococcal</u> <u>antigen</u>, <u>West Nile virus</u> <u>IgM antibody</u> (seasonal)  [[3]](/library/vfdAL60)

* Tests for <u>autoimmune encephalitis</u>: <u>anti-NMDAR antibodies</u>, <u>IgG index</u>, <u>oligoclonal bands</u>

* Additional studies in children < 18 years of age  [[3]](/library/vfdAL60)

* <u>Mycoplasma pneumoniae</u> <u>serology</u>: <u>IgG</u> and <u>IgM antibodies</u>

* <u>EBV serology</u>: <u>anti-VCA IgM and IgG antibodies</u>, <u>anti-EBNA IgG</u>

* Throat or oropharyngeal swabs: <u>multiplex PCR</u> for respiratory pathogens

* Stool or rectal swabs: enteroviral <u>PCR</u>





> [!WARNING]
> <u>CSF</u> <u>PCR</u> may be <u>falsely negative</u> early in the course of <u>HSV encephalitis</u>. If no <u>pathogen</u> is identified on initial testing, check <u>HSV</u> <u>PCR</u> on a repeat <u>CSF</u> sample after 3–7 days. [[3]](/library/vfdAL60)




### <u>Neuroimaging</u> [[2]](/library/R9YlMr)[[3]](/library/vfdAL60)




* <u>Brain</u> <u>MRI</u> with contrast: imaging modality of choice ;  [[2]](/library/R9YlMr)

* Indicated in all patients with suspected encephalitis

* Findings and pattern of neuroradiologic involvement may suggest specific causes, e.g.: [[3]](/library/vfdAL60)

* <u>Temporal lobes</u>: <u>HSV encephalitis</u>, <u>limbic encephalitis</u>

* <u>Basal ganglia</u>, <u>thalamus</u>: <u>West Nile encephalitis</u>, <u>Japanese encephalitis</u>

* <u>Brain stem</u>: <u>Listeria encephalitis</u>, <u>enteroviral encephalitis</u>

* <u>Cerebellum</u>: <u>VZV</u>, <u>EBV</u>

* <u>White matter</u> lesions: <u>acute disseminated encephalomyelitis</u>

* <u>Ischemic</u> lesions: <u>VZV</u>, <u>syphilis</u>, <u>fungal infections</u>, <u>tuberculosis</u>

* <u>Brain</u> CT (with and without contrast): if <u>MRI is contraindicated</u> or not available  [[2]](/library/R9YlMr)





> [!TIP]
> Always consider <u>HSV encephalitis</u> if imaging shows <u>temporal lobe</u> involvement; bilateral <u>temporal lobe</u> abnormality is <u>pathognomonic</u>. [[2]](/library/R9YlMr)




> [!WARNING]
> A normal <u>brain</u> <u>MRI</u> does not exclude encephalitis.




### <u>EEG</u> [[2]](/library/R9YlMr)[[4]](/library/JSds0p0)




* Indication: suspected encephalitis (all patients)

* Findings: usually nonspecific

* Epileptiform discharges from the affected <u>temporal lobes</u> in <u>HSV encephalitis</u>

* <u>Extreme delta brush</u> in <u>anti-NMDA encephalitis</u>





> [!TIP]
> <u>EEG</u> can identify <u>nonconvulsive status epilepticus</u> as a cause of <u>altered mental status</u>.




### Additional investigations for encephalitis [[2]](/library/R9YlMr)[[3]](/library/vfdAL60)[[4]](/library/JSds0p0)




Additional testing is guided by infectious diseases and <u>neurology</u> based on clinical features, exposures, <u>risk factors</u>, and local <u>epidemiology</u>.




* Serum and <u>CSF</u> tests: often performed on prefrozen samples if initial testing is negative

* <u>Infectious causes of encephalitis</u>: testing for additional opportunistic, seasonal, and/or locally <u>endemic</u> infections

* <u>Autoimmune causes of encephalitis</u>: testing for additional <u>autoantibodies</u>

* Other disorders: <u>CSF</u> <u>cytology</u> and <u>flow cytometry</u>, testing for <u>prion disease</u> (e.g., <u>RT-QuIC</u>)

* Other tissue and/or fluid sampling: e.g., for culture, <u>PCR</u>, <u>histology</u>

* Upper respiratory illness: throat swabs

* Pulmonary involvement: <u>sputum</u> and/or <u>bronchoalveolar lavage</u>

* <u>Rash</u>: <u>biopsy</u>

* <u>Diarrhea</u>: stool studies

* <u>Malignancy</u> evaluation: See “Diagnostics” in “<u>Autoimmune encephalitis</u>.”

* <u>Brain biopsy</u>: considered if the cause of encephalitis remains unknown and the patient is clinically deteriorating

---

## Differential diagnoses

See also “<u>Causes of AMS and coma</u>,” “<u>Causes of agitation</u>,” and “<u>Etiology of delirium</u>.”




* <u>Encephalopathies</u>

* <u>Metabolic encephalopathies</u>: e.g., <u>uremic encephalopathy</u>, <u>hepatic encephalopathy</u>, <u>Hashimoto encephalopathy</u>

* <u>HIV encephalopathy</u>

* <u>Wernicke encephalopathy</u>

* <u>Multicystic encephalopathy</u>

* <u>Hypertensive encephalopathy</u>

* <u>Chronic toxic encephalopathy</u>

* <u>Wilson disease</u>

* <u>Anoxic encephalopathy</u>

* <u>Neonatal encephalopathy</u>

* Vascular disorders: e.g., <u>stroke</u>, <u>thrombosis</u>

* Degenerative disorders: e.g., <u>Alzheimer disease</u>, <u>frontotemporal dementia</u>, <u>Prion disease</u>

* Neuropsychiatric disorders: <u>psychosis</u>, <u>Huntington disease</u>

* Other conditions

* <u>Meningitis</u>

* <u>Epilepsy</u>

* <u>Substance intoxication or withdrawal</u>





The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## Initial management

> [!WARNING]
> Encephalitis is a life-threatening disease with nonspecific clinical presentation; treatment delays result in poor outcomes.




### Approach [[2]](/library/R9YlMr)[[3]](/library/vfdAL60)




* Acutely ill patients: Follow the <u>ABCDE approach</u>.

* <u>Airway management and ventilation</u> (e.g., if <u>GCS</u> is < 8)

* <u>Immediate hemodynamic support</u>

* <u>Management of agitation</u>

* <u>Initial stabilization for acute seizures</u>

* <u>Management of elevated intracranial pressure</u> (<u>ICP</u>)

* All patients

* Consult <u>neurology</u> and infectious diseases immediately.

* Initiate immediate <u>empiric antimicrobial therapy for encephalitis</u> before diagnostic confirmation.

* Once etiology is known, tailor cause-specific management under specialist guidance.

* See “Treatment” in “<u>Infectious encephalitis</u>” and “<u>Autoimmune encephalitis</u>” for details.

* Disposition [[8]](/library/5ybifw)

* Admit to the hospital for <u>multidisciplinary care</u>.

* Consider neurological <u>ICU</u> admission for severely ill patients (e.g., with <u>seizures</u>, <u>signs of elevated ICP</u>).





### Empiric antimicrobial therapy for encephalitis [[2]](/library/R9YlMr)[[3]](/library/vfdAL60)




* All patients: Start <u>antimicrobial treatment for HSV encephalitis</u> with IV <u>acyclovir</u>. DOSAGE  [[2]](/library/R9YlMr)[[3]](/library/vfdAL60)

* Possible <u>bacterial meningitis</u>: Add <u>empiric antibiotic therapy for bacterial meningitis</u>.  [[2]](/library/R9YlMr)[[3]](/library/vfdAL60)

* Possible <u>rickettsiosis</u> or <u>ehrlichiosis</u>: Add <u>doxycycline</u> (<u>off-label</u> for <u>ehrlichiosis</u> and for children < 8 years of age). DOSAGE  [[2]](/library/R9YlMr)[[3]](/library/vfdAL60)[[9]](/library/Ef18LT0)





> [!WARNING]
> <u>CSF</u> <u>HSV-1</u> <u>PCR</u> may be <u>falsely negative</u> early in the disease course. If clinical suspicion of <u>HSV encephalitis</u> persists despite an initial negative result, continue IV <u>acyclovir</u> and repeat testing after 3–7 days. [[3]](/library/vfdAL60)




### Empiric immunomodulatory therapy for <u>autoimmune encephalitis</u> [[10]](/library/Ag1RBT0)




* Consider after infectious causes have been excluded.

* See “<u>Treatment of autoimmune encephalitis</u>.”

---

## Infectious encephalitis

### Etiology of infectious encephalitis [[2]](/library/R9YlMr)[[3]](/library/vfdAL60)




#### Viral encephalitis




Viral encephalitis is the most common type of <u>infectious encephalitis</u>.




* <u>Herpesviruses</u>

* <u>Herpes simplex virus type 1</u> (<u>HSV-1</u>): <u>HSV encephalitis</u> (most common cause of encephalitis)

* <u>Herpes simplex virus type 2</u> (<u>HSV-2</u>): <u>HSV encephalitis</u> (in <u>neonates</u> and the <u>immunocompromised</u>)

* <u>Varicella zoster virus</u> (<u>VZV</u>): <u>herpes zoster encephalitis</u>  [[3]](/library/vfdAL60)

* <u>Cytomegalovirus</u> (<u>CMV</u>): <u>CMV encephalitis</u> (most commonly affects <u>immunocompromised individuals</u>, especially those with <u>AIDS</u>)

* <u>Epstein-Barr virus</u> (<u>EBV</u>): <u>EBV</u> encephalitis (most commonly affects children, <u>adolescents</u>, and <u>immunocompromised individuals</u>)  [[3]](/library/vfdAL60)[[4]](/library/JSds0p0)

* Mosquito-borne <u>viruses</u>

* <u>West Nile virus</u>: <u>West Nile encephalitis</u>

* <u>Murray Valley encephalitis virus</u>: <u>Murray Valley encephalitis</u>

* <u>Japanese encephalitis virus</u>: <u>Japanese encephalitis</u>

* <u>St. Louis encephalitis virus</u>: <u>St. Louis encephalitis</u>

* <u>Western equine encephalitis</u> <u>virus</u>: <u>western equine encephalitis</u>

* <u>Eastern equine encephalitis</u> <u>virus</u>: <u>eastern equine encephalitis</u>

* <u>La Crosse virus</u>: <u>La Crosse encephalitis</u>

* <u>California encephalitis virus</u>: <u>California encephalitis</u> [[11]](/library/2RdTmp0)

* Tick-borne virusesOther

* <u>Enteroviruses</u>: <u>enteroviral encephalitis</u>

* Human <u>immunodeficiency</u> <u>viruses</u> (<u>HIV</u>): <u>HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder</u>, <u>acute retroviral syndrome</u>

* <u>Measles virus</u>: encephalitis, <u>subacute sclerosing panencephalitis</u>

* <u>Mumps virus</u>: <u>mumps</u> encephalitis

* <u>Rabies virus</u>: <u>encephalitic rabies</u>





* <u>Tick-borne encephalitis virus</u>: <u>tick-borne encephalitis</u>

* <u>Powassan virus</u>: Powassan encephalitis





#### Bacterial encephalitis




Bacterial encephalitis may be a primary infection or secondary to extracerebral bacterial infection.




* <u>Treponema pallidum</u>: <u>neurosyphilis</u>

* <u>Borrelia burgdorferi</u>: <u>neuroborreliosis</u>

* <u>Listeria monocytogenes</u>: <u>listeria encephalitis</u>

* <u>Rickettsia rickettsii</u>: <u>Rocky Mountain spotted fever</u> (<u>RMSF</u>)

* <u>Ehrlichia</u>: <u>ehrlichiosis</u>

* <u>Mycobacterium tuberculosis</u>: <u>tuberculous meningoencephalitis</u>





#### Fungal encephalitis




* <u>Cryptococcus neoformans</u>: <u>cryptococcal meningoencephalitis</u>

* <u>Coccidioides</u> spp.: <u>coccidioidomycosis</u>

* <u>Histoplasma capsulatum</u>: <u>histoplasmosis</u>





#### Parasitic encephalitis




* <u>Toxoplasma gondii</u>: <u>toxoplasmic encephalitis</u>

* <u>Plasmodium falciparum</u>: cerebral <u>malaria</u>

* <u>Trypanosoma brucei</u>: <u>African trypanosomiasis</u>

* <u>Naegleria fowleri</u>: <u>primary amebic meningoencephalitis</u>





### Risk factors for infectious encephalitis [[2]](/library/R9YlMr)[[3]](/library/vfdAL60)[[5]](/library/Ph1WVg0)




* Travel to <u>endemic</u> areas

* Contact with <u>vector</u> animals and insects (e.g., mosquitoes, ticks)

* Recreational and <u>occupational exposure</u>

* Risky food exposure (e.g., unpasteurized milk or raw/undercooked meat)

* Sick contacts

* <u>Underimmunization</u>

* <u>Risk factors for sexually transmitted infections</u>

* <u>Risk factors for HIV</u> or other immune compromise





### Clinical features




See “<u>Clinical features of encephalitis</u>.”




### Diagnostics [[2]](/library/R9YlMr)[[3]](/library/vfdAL60)




* See “<u>Diagnosis of encephalitis</u>” for a structured approach to the workup of undifferentiated encephalitis.

* Testing for universally common pathogens (e.g., <u>HSV-1</u>, <u>HSV-2</u>, <u>VZV</u>, <u>enteroviruses</u>) is recommended in all patients.

* Testing for additional pathogens is considered based on patient and epidemiological factors.





### Treatment [[2]](/library/R9YlMr)[[3]](/library/vfdAL60)[[4]](/library/JSds0p0)




* Begin <u>initial management of encephalitis</u>.

* Administer <u>empiric antimicrobial therapy for encephalitis</u>.





#### <u>Pathogen</u>-specific treatment




Once the <u>etiology of infectious encephalitis</u> is identified, switch to tailored treatment under infectious diseases specialist guidance(see respective disease articles for dosages).




* Viral

* <u>Treatment of HSV encephalitis</u>;  or <u>antiviral therapy for VZV infection</u>: IV <u>acyclovir</u>

* <u>Treatment of CMV infection</u>: IV <u>ganciclovir</u> PLUS IV <u>foscarnet</u>

* <u>HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder</u>: <u>antiretroviral therapy</u>

* Most other <u>viruses</u>: no specific <u>antiviral therapy</u>; <u>supportive care</u>

* Bacterial

* <u>Meningitis</u>: <u>empiric antibiotics for bacterial meningitis</u>

* <u>Treatment of listeriosis</u>: IV <u>ampicillin</u> PLUS IV <u>gentamicin</u>

* <u>Treatment of neurosyphilis</u>: IV <u>penicillin G</u> OR IV <u>ceftriaxone</u>

* <u>TB meningoencephalitis</u>: extended <u>RIPE TB regimen</u> with adjunctive <u>glucocorticoids</u> (See “<u>Treatment of extrapulmonary TB</u>” for details.)

* See also “<u>Pathogen-specific therapy in meningitis</u>.”

* Tick-borne bacterial

* <u>Lyme neuroborreliosis</u>: IV <u>ceftriaxone</u>, IV <u>cefotaxime</u>, OR IV <u>penicillin G</u>

* <u>RMSF</u> or <u>ehrlichiosis</u>: PO/IV <u>doxycycline</u>

* Fungal

* <u>Cryptococcal meningoencephalitis</u>: <u>amphotericin B</u> PLUS <u>flucytosine</u>

* <u>Coccidioides</u> encephalitis: <u>fluconazole</u>, <u>itraconazole</u>, <u>voriconazole</u>, OR <u>amphotericin B</u>

* <u>Histoplasma</u> encephalitis: <u>amphotericin B</u> followed by <u>itraconazole</u>

* For <u>antifungal</u> dosages, see “<u>Management of systemic fungal infections</u>.”

* Parasitic

* <u>Treatment of cerebral toxoplasmosis</u>: <u>pyrimethamine</u> PLUS <u>sulfadiazine</u> PLUS <u>leucovorin</u> [[12]](/library/05XeiA)

* <u>Treatment of cerebral malaria</u>: IV <u>artesunate</u> followed by PO <u>artemether-lumefantrine</u> [[13]](/library/fnbks8)

* <u>Treatment of African trypanosomiasis</u>: <u>fexinidazole</u> OR a combination of <u>eflornithine</u> PLUS <u>nifurtimox</u> [[14]](/library/VidGqp0)

* <u>Primary amebic meningoencephalitis</u>: IV and intrathecal <u>amphotericin B</u> PLUS <u>rifampin</u> PLUS other agents  [[2]](/library/R9YlMr)[[15]](/library/kWbmls)

---

## Autoimmune encephalitis

### Etiology [[3]](/library/vfdAL60)[[10]](/library/Ag1RBT0)[[16]](/library/_g15BT0)




* Paraneoplastic encephalitis: inflammation of the <u>brain</u> caused by an immune-mediated response to a systemic <u>malignancy</u>

* Nonparaneoplastic <u>autoimmune encephalitis</u>

* <u>Idiopathic</u>

* Postinfectious: e.g., <u>acute disseminated encephalomyelitis</u>, post-<u>HSV encephalitis</u>

* Systemic autoimmune disorders: e.g., <u>SLE</u>, <u>sarcoidosis</u>

* <u>Iatrogenic</u>: caused by immune-modulating agents, e.g., <u>immune checkpoint inhibitors</u>





### Classification of autoimmune encephalitis [[3]](/library/vfdAL60)[[10]](/library/Ag1RBT0)[[16]](/library/_g15BT0)




<u>Autoimmune encephalitis</u> can be classified by etiology, serological findings, or affected anatomic region.




* Etiologic

* <u>Paraneoplastic encephalitis</u>

* Nonparaneoplastic <u>autoimmune encephalitis</u>

* Serologic

* <u>Autoantibody</u>-associated encephalitis: associated with <u>autoantibodies</u> to neuronal intracellular <u>antigens</u> ;  [[10]](/library/Ag1RBT0)

* Anti-Hu antibodies: paraneoplastic <u>brainstem encephalitis</u> often associated with <u>small cell lung cancer</u>

* Anti-Yo antibodies: paraneoplastic <u>cerebellar</u> encephalitis often associated with gynecologic and <u>breast malignancies</u>

* Anti-Tr antibodies: paraneoplastic <u>cerebellar</u> encephalitis often associated with <u>Hodgkin lymphoma</u>

* <u>Autoantibody</u>-mediated encephalitis: mediated by <u>autoantibodies</u> to neuronal surface <u>antigens</u> ;  [[10]](/library/Ag1RBT0)

* <u>Anti-NMDAR antibodies</u>; : <u>paraneoplastic encephalitis</u> (e.g., due to ovarian <u>teratoma</u>), post-<u>HSV encephalitis</u>

* <u>VGKC-complex antibodies</u>: nonparaneoplastic <u>limbic encephalitis</u>

* Seronegative <u>autoimmune encephalitis</u>: not associated with identifiable <u>autoantibodies</u>

* Anatomic

* <u>Limbic encephalitis</u>

* <u>Cerebellitis</u>

* <u>Brainstem encephalitis</u>





### Clinical features [[10]](/library/Ag1RBT0)[[17]](/library/yg1dBT0)




General <u>clinical features of encephalitis</u> are usually present. The following features are more suggestive of <u>autoimmune encephalitis</u>:




* Subacute or chronic onset

* Clinical features of underlying etiology, e.g.:

* <u>Malignancy</u>, e.g., <u>constitutional symptoms</u>

* Recent viral illness

* Autoimmune disease (e.g., <u>clinical features of SLE</u>)

* Prominent psychiatric and neurological manifestations (e.g., in anti-NDMAR encephalitis and <u>limbic encephalitis</u>)





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Autoimmune encephalitis</u> cannot be distinguished from <u>infectious encephalitis</u> based on clinical features alone. [[10]](/library/Ag1RBT0)[[17]](/library/yg1dBT0)




### Diagnostics [[3]](/library/vfdAL60)[[10]](/library/Ag1RBT0)




See “<u>Diagnosis of encephalitis</u>” for a structured approach to the workup of undifferentiated encephalitis.




* Routine investigations

* Test all patients for <u>anti-NMDAR antibodies</u> (in serum and <u>CSF</u>), <u>IgG index</u>, and <u>oligoclonal bands</u>.

* Consider <u>paraneoplastic panel</u> testing in serum and <u>CSF</u> based on availability and local protocols.

* Further testing

* Consider testing for additional <u>autoantibodies</u> in consultation with <u>neurology</u>.

* See “<u>Classification of autoimmune encephalitis</u>” for specific <u>antibodies</u>.

* Evaluation for underlying <u>malignancy</u>: Consider in all adults with confirmed or suspected <u>autoimmune encephalitis</u>.

* CT chest, abdomen, and <u>pelvis</u>

* <u>Mammography</u>, <u>pelvic</u> <u>ultrasound</u>

* Whole body <u>PET-CT scan</u> if initial evaluation is negative





### Treatment of autoimmune encephalitis [[10]](/library/Ag1RBT0)




* Approach

* For preliminary steps, see “<u>Initial treatment of encephalitis</u>.”

* If clinical suspicion is high, consider empiric therapy prior to diagnostic confirmation once infectious causes are excluded.  [[10]](/library/Ag1RBT0)

* Consult a specialist (e.g., <u>neurology</u>) for guidance on treatment options.

* Consider neurological <u>ICU</u> admission for severely ill patients (e.g., with <u>seizures</u>, <u>signs of elevated ICP</u>).

* All patients: immunomodulatory therapy

* First-line: high-dose <u>corticosteroids</u>, <u>intravenous immunoglobulin</u>, <u>plasmapheresis</u>

* Second-line: <u>rituximab</u>, <u>cyclophosphamide</u>

* <u>Paraneoplastic encephalitis</u>: immunomodulatory treatment and treatment of the underlying <u>malignancy</u> (e.g., <u>tumor</u> resection)





### Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis [[3]](/library/vfdAL60)[[17]](/library/yg1dBT0)[[18]](/library/ujdpXJ0)




* <u>Epidemiology</u> [[3]](/library/vfdAL60)

* Most common type of <u>autoimmune encephalitis</u>

* Most common in children and young adults

* <u>♀</u>:<u>♂</u> = 4:1

* Etiology

* Approx. 50% of cases are paraneoplastic. [[3]](/library/vfdAL60)

* Often associated with ovarian <u>teratoma</u>

* May develop as a complication of <u>HSV encephalitis</u>  [[4]](/library/JSds0p0)[[19]](/library/npd7JI0)

* Clinical features: similar to the general <u>clinical features of encephalitis</u> with prominent psychiatric and neurological manifestations

* Cognitive and behavioral abnormalities: e.g., <u>psychosis</u>, <u>agitation</u>, <u>catatonia</u>

* <u>Memory</u> deficits

* Speech dysfunction

* <u>Dyskinesias</u> and/or <u>seizures</u>

* <u>Autonomic dysfunction</u>

* Decreased <u>level of consciousness</u>

* Diagnostics: See “<u>Diagnosis of encephalitis</u>” for a structured approach to the workup of undifferentiated encephalitis.

* <u>Confirmatory test</u>: positive anti-NMDA receptor antibodies in <u>CSF</u>  [[17]](/library/yg1dBT0)

* <u>CSF analysis</u>: <u>WBC count</u> usually < 50/mmÂ³

* <u>Brain</u> <u>MRI</u>: may be normal

* <u>EEG</u>

* Slowing, <u>epileptogenic</u> activity

* Extreme delta brush: a <u>pathognomonic</u> pattern resembling waveforms seen in <u>premature infants</u>

* <u>Malignancy</u> evaluation: e.g., <u>transvaginal ultrasonography</u> to evaluate for ovarian <u>teratoma</u>

* Treatment

* Immunomodulatory therapy (See “<u>Treatment of autoimmune encephalitis</u>.”)

* Treatment of the underlying <u>tumor</u> (e.g., removal of ovarian <u>teratoma</u>) may be curative.





### Limbic encephalitis [[16]](/library/_g15BT0)[[17]](/library/yg1dBT0)




* Definition: inflammation of <u>brain</u> tissue that primarily affects the <u>limbic system</u> in the <u>medial</u> <u>temporal lobes</u>

* Pathophysiology: caused by an autoimmune reaction with <u>antibodies</u> directed against <u>antigens</u> richly expressed in the <u>limbic system</u>

* Etiology [[20]](/library/WJdPGI0)

* Most often paraneoplastic: associated with <u>SCLC</u> (most common), <u>breast cancer</u>, <u>testicular cancer</u>

* Also associated with infections (e.g., <u>HSV infection</u>) and systemic autoimmune conditions (e.g., <u>SLE</u>, <u>systemic sclerosis</u>)

* Clinical features: similar to the general <u>clinical features of encephalitis</u> with prominent psychiatric and neurological manifestations

* Severe <u>short-term memory</u> impairment

* <u>Seizures</u>

* Confusion

* Psychiatric symptoms (e.g., <u>depression</u>, <u>hallucinations</u>, <u>anxiety</u>)

* Diagnosis: See “<u>Diagnosis of encephalitis</u>” for a structured approach to the workup of undifferentiated encephalitis.

* <u>Confirmatory test</u>: characteristic <u>autoantibodies</u> (e.g., VGKC-complex antibodies, anti-AMPA receptor antibodies)  [[17]](/library/yg1dBT0)

* <u>CSF analysis</u>: <u>WBC</u> > 5/mmÂ³

* <u>Brain</u> <u>MRI</u>: abnormalities in the bilateral <u>medial</u> <u>temporal lobes</u>

* <u>EEG</u>: <u>epileptogenic</u> or slow-wave activity in the <u>temporal lobes</u>

* <u>Malignancy</u> evaluation: e.g., CT chest to evaluate for <u>SCLC</u>

* Treatment

* Immunomodulatory therapy (See “<u>Treatment of autoimmune encephalitis</u>.”)

* Treatment of the underlying <u>malignancy</u> (e.g., <u>treatment of lung cancer</u>)
